module_title: Feed Cost Optimization and Economic Considerations

lessons.title: Least-Cost Formulation Principles
lessons.body:
Feed is the biggest cost in poultry farming, often 65-75% of total production cost. Least-cost formulation means mixing ingredients to meet the bird's nutrient needs at the lowest possible price per ton. It does not mean using the cheapest ingredients alone; it means balancing nutrients and cost. You need to know the nutrient requirements of your birds (e.g., 20% crude protein for broiler starter), the nutrient content of available ingredients (e.g., maize 8.5% protein, soybean meal 44% protein), and the current prices per kg.

Start by listing all ingredients you can buy, their prices, and their nutrient composition. Then set the minimum and maximum levels for each ingredient. For example, maize can be 50-70% of the diet, soybean meal 20-35%, fishmeal 0-5%, and so on. The goal is to find the combination that meets the nutrient specs at the lowest cost. You can do this manually with simple algebra or using a spreadsheet like Excel Solver, or free tools like WinFeed or FeedSoft. In Africa, many small mills use Excel because it's cheap and available.

A practical example: You want 1000 kg of broiler finisher feed with 18% protein. Maize costs $0.30/kg, soybean meal $0.60/kg, and fishmeal $1.20/kg. If you use too much soybean, cost rises; too much maize, protein drops. The least-cost mix might be 65% maize, 28% soybean, 5% fishmeal, and 2% premix. That gives about 18.2% protein and costs around $0.42/kg. If you simply used equal parts, cost would be higher and protein might not match.

Key principles: always check nutrient specs first, use local ingredients when cheaper, and re-calculate whenever prices change. Keep records of prices and formulations. Remember, least-cost is not fixed; it changes with market prices. So you must update your formulation regularly. Also, consider availability and quality; a cheap ingredient that is often unavailable or of poor quality can disrupt production. Finally, involve a nutritionist if possible, but with training, you can do it yourself.

lessons.title: Using Alternative Ingredients to Reduce Cost
lessons.body:
In many African countries, conventional feed ingredients like maize and soybean meal are expensive or scarce. Alternative ingredients can cut costs by 20-40% if used correctly. Examples include cassava peels, palm kernel cake (PKC), brewers' dried grains (BDG), cottonseed cake, sunflower cake, and even insect meal like black soldier fly larvae. These are often locally available at lower prices. However, they have limitations: high fibre, anti-nutritional factors, or low protein. You must know their nutrient profiles and maximum inclusion rates.

For instance, cassava peels can replace part of maize but are low in protein (2-3%) and high in fibre. You can include up to 20% in broiler diets if you add enzymes or extra protein. Palm kernel cake has 14-18% protein but high fibre; limit to 10-15% for broilers, 20% for layers. Brewers' dried grains have 25-30% protein but also high fibre; use 10-20%. Cottonseed cake has 32-40% protein but contains gossypol, toxic to poultry; limit to 5-10% and use only for layers, not breeders. Sunflower cake has 28-30% protein but high fibre; use up to 15%. Black soldier fly larvae are 40-45% protein and can replace fishmeal, but production is still small-scale in many areas.

To use alternatives, start with small trials. Replace 5-10% of the conventional ingredient and observe bird performance (weight gain, feed intake, egg production). Adjust gradually. Always balance for energy, protein, amino acids, and minerals. You may need to add synthetic amino acids like lysine and methionine, or enzymes like phytase to improve digestibility. For example, if you use 15% PKC, you might need to add 0.1% lysine and 0.05% methionine. Also, check for mycotoxins, especially in cottonseed and groundnut cake. Store alternatives properly to prevent mould.

Cost savings come from lower ingredient cost per ton. But if performance drops, the savings may be lost. So calculate cost per kg of weight gain or per egg, not just per ton of feed. In Kenya, farmers using cassava peels and BDG have reduced feed cost by 25% without hurting performance. In Nigeria, PKC-based diets cut costs by 30% for layers. Always source from reliable suppliers and test each batch for nutrient content. With practice, you can create least-cost diets using a mix of conventional and alternative ingredients.

lessons.title: Impact of Ingredient Prices on Formulation Decisions
lessons.body:
Ingredient prices change constantly due to season, fuel costs, import policies, and global markets. A formulation that is least-cost today may be too expensive next month. So you must monitor prices weekly and adjust your feed mix. For example, maize price in Nigeria often rises 30-50% during the dry season (January-March) when stocks are low. Soybean meal prices may spike when import bans or currency devaluation occur. Fishmeal is expensive and volatile; in 2022, it cost $1.50-$2.00/kg in many African markets, while locally produced alternatives like black soldier fly meal cost $0.80-$1.20/kg.

When prices change, you need to re-run your least-cost formulation. Suppose your original mix uses 60% maize, 30% soybean meal, and 10% fishmeal. If maize price doubles, you might replace some maize with cassava peels or wheat bran. If soybean meal becomes very expensive, you might use more cottonseed cake or sunflower cake, but you must add amino acids. The key is to have a list of alternative ingredients with their prices and nutrient specs ready. Use a spreadsheet that automatically recalculates the cheapest mix when you update prices. Excel Solver or free apps like Feed Formulation (Android) can do this.

Price changes also affect the decision to buy in bulk. If you expect maize prices to rise, buy and store enough for 2-3 months, but ensure proper storage to avoid aflatoxin. If prices are high, consider reducing the nutrient density slightly (e.g., 1% less protein) if it doesn't hurt performance too much. But be careful: lower nutrient density may increase feed intake and total cost. Always calculate cost per kg of gain or per egg. For layers, a 1% drop in protein might reduce egg size but save 5% on feed cost; test if profitable.

In Africa, government policies like import tariffs on maize or soybean meal can suddenly change prices. Stay informed through market bulletins, radio, or farmer groups. Also, consider contract farming or cooperative buying to get better prices. For example, a cooperative in Ghana buys maize in bulk during harvest and stores it, saving 20% compared to buying monthly. Finally, keep a record of price trends to predict future changes. If you see a pattern, you can plan your formulation and purchasing strategy accordingly.

lessons.title: Linear Programming for Cost Minimization
lessons.body:
Linear programming (LP) is a mathematical method to find the cheapest combination of ingredients that meets all nutrient requirements. It is the engine behind least-cost formulation software. You don't need to be a mathematician; you just need to set up the problem correctly. The basic idea: you have a set of ingredients, each with a cost and nutrient content. You have a set of constraints: minimum and maximum levels for each nutrient (e.g., protein â¥ 18%, calcium â¥ 0.9%) and for each ingredient (e.g., maize â¤ 70%, fishmeal â¤ 5%). The LP solver finds the amounts of each ingredient that minimize total cost while satisfying all constraints.

In practice, you can use Microsoft Excel with the Solver add-in. Here's how: List ingredients in rows, and nutrients in columns. In one row, put the cost per kg. In the cells below, put the nutrient composition (e.g., protein, fat, fibre, calcium, phosphorus, lysine, methionine). Then create a column for the amount of each ingredient (in kg or %). The total cost is the sum of amount times cost. The total nutrient is the sum of amount times nutrient content. Set the target cell (total cost) to minimize. Add constraints: total amount = 1000 kg (or 100%), each nutrient â¥ or â¤ the required level, each ingredient â¥ or â¤ its limit. Solver will find the optimal amounts.

For example, in a broiler starter diet, you might have maize, soybean meal, fishmeal, wheat bran, limestone, and premix. Constraints: protein â¥ 20%, metabolizable energy â¥ 2900 kcal/kg, calcium 0.9-1.0%, available phosphorus 0.45%, lysine â¥ 1.1%, methionine â¥ 0.5%. Ingredient limits: maize 50-65%, soybean meal 20-35%, fishmeal 0-5%, wheat bran 0-10%, limestone 1-1.5%, premix 0.25%. Solver will give you the cheapest mix. If Solver is not available, you can use free online LP solvers or apps like WinFeed, which are designed for animal feed.

LP is powerful because it considers all ingredients and constraints at once, unlike manual trial-and-error. It also gives a shadow price for each nutrient, telling you how much cost would increase if you tightened a constraint. This helps you decide if you can relax a nutrient spec to save money. For example, if the shadow price of protein is high, you might reduce protein by 0.5% and save $10 per ton. However, you must ensure the bird's performance is not compromised. Always validate the LP result with a small feeding trial. With practice, LP becomes a quick and reliable tool for cost minimization.

lessons.title: Evaluating Cost per Unit of Nutrient vs. Cost per Ton
lessons.body:
Many farmers compare feed costs by looking at price per ton or per bag. But that is misleading because feeds differ in nutrient density. A cheaper feed per ton may actually be more expensive per unit of protein, energy, or amino acid. The correct way is to calculate cost per unit of nutrient, such as cost per kg of crude protein, cost per 1000 kcal of metabolizable energy, or cost per kg of lysine. This allows you to compare ingredients or complete feeds fairly.

For example, suppose maize costs $300/ton and contains 8.5% protein. Cost per kg protein = $300 / (1000 kg * 0.085) = $3.53/kg protein. Soybean meal costs $600/ton and contains 44% protein. Cost per kg protein = $600 / (1000 * 0.44) = $1.36/kg protein. So despite being more expensive per ton, soybean meal is much cheaper per unit of protein. Similarly, fishmeal at $1200/ton with 65% protein gives $1.85/kg protein, still cheaper than maize. This shows why you cannot judge by ton price alone.

When evaluating a complete feed, calculate the cost per kg of protein or per 1000 kcal. For a broiler starter with 20% protein, if it costs $450/ton, cost per kg protein = $450 / (1000 * 0.20) = $2.25/kg. Another feed with 18% protein at $400/ton gives $400 / (1000 * 0.18) = $2.22/kg. The second is slightly cheaper per unit protein, but you must also check energy and amino acids. Often, a more nutrient-dense feed is more cost-effective because birds eat less and grow faster. For layers, calculate cost per kg of egg or per dozen eggs.

To do this, you need the nutrient composition of your ingredients or feed. Use a feed analysis table or send samples to a lab. Then, for each ingredient, compute cost per unit of the most limiting nutrient. In Africa, where protein is often expensive, focus on cost per kg of protein and cost per kg of lysine and methionine. Also consider energy: cost per 1000 kcal ME. For example, palm oil is expensive per ton but high in energy; cost per 1000 kcal may be lower than maize. Use a spreadsheet to compare. This method helps you choose the most economical ingredients and justify using alternatives. It also helps you explain to buyers why your feed is priced higher but gives better value.

lessons.title: Case Study: Optimizing a Broiler Diet Under Price Volatility
lessons.body:
In 2023, a small poultry farm in Uganda faced volatile prices: maize jumped from $0.25/kg to $0.40/kg due to drought, while soybean meal rose from $0.55/kg to $0.70/kg. Fishmeal was $1.30/kg. The farm needed to produce broiler finisher feed (18% protein, 3000 kcal ME/kg) for 1000 birds. The original formulation was 60% maize, 30% soybean meal, 5% fishmeal, 3% wheat bran, 1% limestone, 0.5% premix, and 0.5% salt. Cost per ton was $420. With new prices, the same mix cost $510 per ton, a 21% increase. The farm wanted to reduce cost without hurting performance.

The manager used Excel Solver to re-optimize. Constraints: protein â¥ 18%, ME â¥ 3000 kcal/kg, calcium 0.9-1.0%, available phosphorus â¥ 0.45%, lysine â¥ 1.0%, methionine â¥ 0.45%. Ingredient limits: maize 40-65%, soybean meal 15-30%, fishmeal 0-5%, wheat bran 0-15%, cassava peels 0-15%, palm kernel cake 0-10%, limestone 1-1.5%, premix 0.25%, salt 0.25%. The solver found a new mix: 50% maize, 20% soybean meal, 3% fishmeal, 10% wheat bran, 12% cassava peels, 3% palm kernel cake, 1.2% limestone, 0.3% premix, 0.5% salt. This mix met all nutrients and cost $440 per ton, a 14% saving from the original adjusted cost. The farm also added 0.1% lysine and 0.05% methionine to balance amino acids.

They conducted a small trial with 100 birds on the new diet and 100 on the old diet. After 4 weeks, the new diet group had similar weight gain (1.8 kg vs 1.82 kg) and feed conversion ratio (1.65 vs 1.63). Feed cost per kg gain was $0.73 for the new diet vs $0.83 for the old, saving $0.10 per kg. For 1000 birds, that's a saving of $180. The farm also learned to buy cassava peels and palm kernel cake in bulk during harvest when prices are low. They now monitor prices weekly and re-run the formulation when any ingredient price changes by more than 10%. This case shows that with simple tools and local alternatives, you can maintain profitability even when prices fluctuate. Key lessons: use least-cost software, test alternatives gradually, and always calculate cost per kg of gain, not just per ton.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Feed Cost Optimization and Economic Considerations

Feed represents 65â75% of the total cost of producing a kilogram of broiler meat or a dozen eggs in most African poultry enterprises. For a commercial farm in Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, or South Africa, a 5% reduction in feed cost per tonne can translate directly into a 3â4% improvement in net margin â often the difference between profit and loss. This practical reference consolidates the core principles of least-cost formulation, alternative ingredient use, price sensitivity, linear programming, nutrient-cost evaluation, and volatility management into a single working document for farm managers, feed millers, and agribusiness advisors.

1. Least-Cost Formulation Principles

Least-cost formulation is not about buying the cheapest ingredients â it is about meeting the bird's nutrient requirements at the lowest possible cost per unit of nutrient delivered. The core principle is simple: the value of an ingredient is determined by its nutrient content relative to its price, not by its price alone. A tonne of maize at US$280 may be cheaper than a tonne of cassava chips at US$200, but if the cassava chips require additional synthetic amino acids and enzyme supplementation to match maize's energy density, the true cost per megajoule of metabolizable energy (ME) may be higher.

In practice, least-cost formulation requires three inputs: (1) a nutrient specification matrix for each ingredient (ME, crude protein, lysine, methionine, calcium, available phosphorus, etc.), (2) a set of nutrient constraints for the target bird class (starter, grower, finisher, layer phase 1â3), and (3) current market prices for all available ingredients. The formulation algorithm then selects the combination that minimizes total cost while satisfying all constraints. In Africa, where ingredient quality varies widely, regular laboratory analysis of local ingredients is essential â book values from international tables often overestimate nutrient content of locally sourced maize, soy cake, or fishmeal.

2. Using Alternative Ingredients to Reduce Cost

Africa has a rich supply of alternative feed ingredients that are underutilized in commercial poultry diets. These include cassava chips, sweet potato meal, palm kernel cake, cottonseed cake, groundnut cake, sunflower cake, brewers' dried grains, molasses, and various leaf meals (e.g., Moringa oleifera, Leucaena). The key is to use them within safe inclusion limits and with appropriate enzyme or amino acid supplementation.

3. Impact of Ingredient Prices on Formulation Decisions

Ingredient prices in Africa are volatile due to currency fluctuations, import dependency (especially for soy and fishmeal), seasonal harvest cycles, and logistical constraints. A 10% increase in maize price can shift the optimal inclusion of cassava chips upward by 5â8 percentage points in a broiler diet. Similarly, a spike in soy cake price often triggers increased use of groundnut cake, cottonseed cake, or synthetic amino acids to maintain protein and lysine levels.

The practical implication is that formulation should not be static. Feed millers should re-run least-cost formulations weekly or bi-weekly, or whenever a key ingredient price moves by more than 5%. Sensitivity analysis â testing how the optimal mix changes when key prices vary by Â±10% â is a powerful tool for anticipating changes before they occur.

Source: Author's calculations based on feed formulation principles and indicative African market prices (2024â2025). Actual costs vary by country, season, and supplier.

4. Linear Programming for Cost Minimization

Linear programming (LP) is the mathematical engine behind least-cost formulation. The objective function is to minimize total feed cost (sum of ingredient quantities Ã prices), subject to constraints: nutrient requirements (minimum and maximum levels), ingredient inclusion limits, and availability. Modern feed formulation software (e.g., WinFeed, Bestmix, Brill, or open-source tools like R) solves these problems in seconds.

For small and medium African feed millers, LP can be implemented even in a spreadsheet (Excel Solver) with 10â20 ingredients and 15â25 nutrient constraints. The key is accurate data: ingredient nutrient composition, prices, and bird requirements. Where laboratory analysis is not available, use conservative book values and build in safety margins.

5. Evaluating Cost per Unit of Nutrient vs. Cost per Tonne

The most common mistake in African feed purchasing is comparing ingredients on a cost-per-tonne basis. The correct metric is cost per unit of the limiting nutrient â usually metabolizable energy (ME) or digestible lysine. For example:

  • Maize at US$280/t with 3,350 kcal ME/kg = US$0.084 per 1,000 kcal ME
  • Cassava chips at US$200/t with 2,950 kcal ME/kg = US$0.068 per 1,000 kcal ME

On a cost-per-tonne basis, cassava looks cheaper. On a cost-per-unit-of-energy basis, cassava is also cheaper â but only if the diet can accommodate its lower protein and higher fibre. When protein supplementation costs are included, the advantage may disappear. Always evaluate ingredients on a nutrient-cost basis, and always consider the full diet context.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Aflatoxin and Mycotoxin Risk

Alternative ingredients such as groundnut cake, cottonseed cake, and maize are highly susceptible to aflatoxin contamination, especially in humid African climates with poor storage. Aflatoxin B1 is a potent carcinogen and causes liver damage, reduced growth, and immunosuppression in poultry. Never use mouldy or discoloured ingredients. Test every batch of high-risk ingredients for aflatoxin (using rapid test kits or laboratory analysis) and reject any batch exceeding 20 ppb total aflatoxin for poultry feed. Use a proven mycotoxin binder (e.g., hydrated sodium calcium aluminosilicate or yeast cell wall products) in finished feed, and store ingredients in dry, well-ventilated conditions with moisture below 12%. Failure to manage mycotoxins can wipe out the entire economic benefit of using cheaper alternative ingredients.

6. Case Study: Optimizing a Broiler Diet Under Price Volatility

A commercial broiler farm in Ghana, producing 20,000 birds per cycle, faced a 25% increase in maize price and a 15% increase in soy cake price over six months. The farm's original finisher diet cost US$430 per tonne. Using least-cost formulation with LP, the farm manager introduced cassava chips (25%), palm kernel cake (8%), and supplemented with synthetic lysine and methionine, plus a phytase enzyme. The new diet met all nutrient requirements (ME 3,100 kcal/kg, CP 18%, digestible lysine 0.85%) at a cost of US$385 per tonne â a saving of US$45 per tonne, or US$10,800 per cycle (assuming 240 tonnes per cycle). The farm also implemented weekly price monitoring and re-formulated whenever key ingredient prices moved by more than 5%. Over 12 months, the farm reduced feed cost per kilogram of live weight from US$0.92 to US$0.83, improving net margin by approximately 18%.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Analyze local ingredients regularly â do not rely solely on book values; nutrient content varies by source, season, and processing.
  2. Formulate on cost per unit of nutrient (ME, lysine, methionine, calcium, available phosphorus), not cost per tonne.
  3. Re-run least-cost formulations weekly or whenever a key ingredient price changes by more than 5%.
  4. Use alternative ingredients within safe inclusion limits and supplement with enzymes, amino acids, or mycotoxin binders as needed.
  5. Test every batch of high-risk ingredients (maize, groundnut cake, cottonseed cake) for aflatoxin before use.
  6. Maintain a price database for at least 10â15 ingredients and update it at least monthly.
  7. Run sensitivity analysis to anticipate how price changes affect the optimal mix and total cost.
  8. Track cost per kilogram of live weight or per egg â not just feed cost per tonne â to measure true economic impact.

Further Reading

  • FAO (2013) â Poultry Development Review â comprehensive open-access review of poultry feed resources and nutrition in developing countries.
  • FAO â Feed Formulation and Least-Cost Diet Principles â practical guidance on feed formulation for small and medium-scale producers.
  • ILRI â International Livestock Research Institute Publications â research on alternative feed ingredients and feed systems in Africa.
  • AfricaBio â Poultry Feed Resources â regional resources on feed ingredient availability and quality.
  • World's Poultry Science Association (WPSA) â scientific journals and technical articles on poultry nutrition and feed formulation.

This practical reference is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course "Broiler and Layer Feed Formulation," Module: Feed Cost Optimization and Economic Considerations. For training and advisory support, contact your local Rise AFRICA hub.

quiz.q: What percentage of total poultry production cost is typically attributed to feed?
quiz.explanation: Feed is the largest cost in poultry production, often accounting for 65-75% of total costs.

quiz.q: What is the primary goal of least-cost formulation?
options: A) To use only the cheapest ingredients
B) To meet nutrient requirements at the lowest cost per ton
D) To minimize the number of ingredients
quiz.explanation: Least-cost formulation aims to meet the bird's nutrient needs at the lowest possible cost, not just using cheap ingredients.

quiz.q: Which tool is commonly used by small mills in Africa for least-cost formulation?
quiz.explanation: Excel with Solver is widely used because it is affordable and available.

quiz.q: In the example, what is the approximate cost per kg of a least-cost broiler finisher mix?
quiz.explanation: The example mix costs around $0.42/kg.

quiz.q: Why must least-cost formulations be updated regularly?
options: A) Because bird nutrient requirements change daily
quiz.explanation: Ingredient prices change frequently, so the least-cost mix must be recalculated.

quiz.q: Which alternative ingredient can replace part of maize but is low in protein and high in fibre?
quiz.explanation: Cassava peels are low in protein (2-3%) and high in fibre, but can replace some maize.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended inclusion rate of palm kernel cake in broiler diets?
quiz.explanation: Palm kernel cake is high in fibre, so it should be limited to 10-15% in broiler diets.

quiz.q: Which anti-nutritional factor is found in cottonseed cake?
quiz.explanation: Cottonseed cake contains gossypol, which is toxic to poultry, so it must be limited.

quiz.q: What is a good strategy when using alternative ingredients?
options: A) Replace all conventional ingredients at once
B) Start with small trials and gradually increase inclusion
D) Use only one alternative ingredient
quiz.explanation: Gradual introduction allows you to monitor performance and adjust as needed.

quiz.q: Which enzyme can be added to improve digestibility of alternative ingredients?
quiz.explanation: Phytase helps release phosphorus from plant ingredients, improving digestibility.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to compare the cost of two feeds?
options: C) Cost per unit of nutrient
D) Cost per kg of feed
quiz.explanation: Comparing cost per unit of nutrient (e.g., per kg protein) gives a fair comparison.

quiz.q: If maize costs $300/ton and has 8.5% protein, what is the cost per kg of protein?
Which ingredient is cheaper per unit of protein: maize at $300/ton (8.5% protein) or soybean meal at $600/ton (44% protein)?
quiz.explanation: Soybean meal costs $1.36/kg protein vs maize at $3.53/kg protein.

quiz.q: What does a high shadow price for protein in linear programming indicate?
options: B) Relaxing the protein constraint could save money
quiz.explanation: A high shadow price means that loosening the protein constraint would reduce cost significantly.

quiz.q: In Excel Solver, what is the target cell set to?
quiz.explanation: The target cell is the total cost, which is minimized.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a constraint in a least-cost formulation?
quiz.explanation: Nutrient requirements like protein â¥ 18% are constraints.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of linear programming over manual formulation?
options: A) It is faster and considers all constraints simultaneously
C) It always uses the cheapest ingredient
quiz.explanation: LP quickly finds the optimal mix while satisfying all constraints.

quiz.q: Which free software is mentioned for feed formulation?
quiz.explanation: WinFeed is a free feed formulation software mentioned in the lesson.

quiz.q: Why is cost per ton misleading when comparing feeds?
options: C) It is not used in Africa
quiz.explanation: A cheaper feed per ton may have lower nutrient density, making it more expensive per unit of nutrient.

quiz.q: For layers, what is a better measure than cost per ton?
options: A) Cost per kg of feed
quiz.explanation: Cost per dozen eggs reflects the true economic value of the feed.

quiz.q: What is the first step in evaluating cost per unit of nutrient?
options: B) Obtain nutrient composition of ingredients
quiz.explanation: You need nutrient composition to calculate cost per unit of nutrient.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is often the most expensive to supply in African poultry diets?
quiz.explanation: Protein sources like soybean meal and fishmeal are expensive, so cost per kg protein is critical.

quiz.q: In the case study, what was the original cost per ton of the broiler finisher feed?
quiz.explanation: The original formulation cost $420 per ton before price increases.

quiz.q: What was the new cost per ton after optimization in the case study?
quiz.explanation: The optimized mix cost $440 per ton, saving 14% from the adjusted cost.

quiz.q: Which alternative ingredient was used in the optimized mix in the case study?
options: A) Cassava peels and palm kernel cake
quiz.explanation: The new mix included cassava peels and palm kernel cake to reduce cost.

quiz.q: What was the feed cost per kg gain for the new diet in the case study?
quiz.explanation: The new diet cost $0.73 per kg gain, compared to $0.83 for the old diet.

quiz.q: What did the farm do after the trial?
options: A) Reverted to the old diet
B) Monitored prices weekly and re-ran formulation when prices changed by >10%
quiz.explanation: They adopted a strategy of regular price monitoring and reformulation.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key lesson from the case study?
options: A) Always use the cheapest ingredients regardless of nutrients
B) Use least-cost software and test alternatives gradually
D) Ignore cost per kg of gain
quiz.explanation: The case study showed the value of least-cost software and gradual testing.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum inclusion of fishmeal in broiler diets?
quiz.explanation: Fishmeal is expensive and typically limited to 0-5% in broiler diets.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of using cheap but poor-quality ingredients?
options: B) They can reduce bird performance and increase total cost
D) They are hard to store
quiz.explanation: Poor quality can lead to poor performance, negating cost savings.
